note: Authored teaching structure per lesson: ordered sections (explain/example/practice/note). Vocabulary and sentence links are derived by the loader from canonical knowledge, never duplicated here.

n5-sentence-order.heading: Predicates close the sentence
n5-sentence-order.body: Japanese orders phrases as topic, then information, then the predicate. The predicate carries tense and polarity, so it always comes last.

n5-sentence-order.heading: Particles assign the role
n5-sentence-order.body: Because word order is flexible, particles identify what each phrase does. 私は and 私が are not interchangeable.

n5-sentence-order.heading: Build three sentences
n5-sentence-order.body: Describe yourself, an object near you, and a classmate. Keep each sentence to topic plus predicate.

n5-particles-wa-ga-o.heading: は sets the topic
n5-particles-wa-ga-o.body: は marks what the sentence is about and often contrasts with something else. It does not mark the grammatical subject.

n5-particles-wa-ga-o.heading: が identifies, を marks the object
n5-particles-wa-ga-o.body: が introduces new or focused information such as who likes something. を marks the direct object of a transitive verb.

n5-particles-wa-ga-o.heading: Preference takes が
n5-particles-wa-ga-o.body: 好き and 嫌い are adjectives, so the liked thing is marked with が rather than を.

n5-polite-verbs.heading: Find the ます stem first
n5-polite-verbs.body: Every polite verb starts from the continuative stem. 食べる becomes 食べ, 行く becomes 行き.

n5-polite-verbs.heading: Tense and polarity live in ます
n5-polite-verbs.body: ます, ません, ました and ませんでした cover the four basic polite forms without changing the stem.

n5-polite-verbs.heading: Conjugate a daily routine
n5-polite-verbs.body: Describe yesterday, today and tomorrow using three different verbs in the polite form.

n5-everyday-requests.heading: The て-form opens requests
n5-everyday-requests.body: Attach ください to the て-form to ask someone to act. The negative request uses ないでください.
examples: 写真を撮らないでください。

n5-everyday-requests.heading: Permission with てもいい
n5-everyday-requests.body: てもいいですか asks whether an action is permitted. A natural reply is どうぞ or すみませんが、ちょっと…

n5-everyday-requests.heading: Directness depends on relationship
n5-everyday-requests.body: てください is polite but directional. With a superior, prefer a softer form or a full polite request.

n4-reasons-kara-node.heading: から states your reason
n4-reasons-kara-node.body: から presents a reason the speaker is committing to, which is why it supports requests and decisions.
examples: 危ないから、止まってください。

n4-reasons-kara-node.heading: ので presents background
n4-reasons-kara-node.body: ので frames the reason as given information. Nouns and na-adjectives take な before ので.
examples: 学生なので、安く買えます。

n4-reasons-kara-node.heading: Contrast the same reason twice
n4-reasons-kara-node.body: Write one request using から and one explanation using ので with the identical reason.

n4-conditionals.heading: たら treats the condition as done
n4-conditionals.body: Because たら uses the past form, the condition is imagined as completed before the result appears.
examples: 雨が降ったら、行きません。

n4-conditionals.heading: ば is general, なら takes context
n4-conditionals.body: ば expresses a general cause and effect and resists commands. なら picks up what the listener just said.
examples: 日本語なら、田中さんが詳しい。

n4-conditionals.heading: Choose by time and control
n4-conditionals.body: For one-off events use たら, for rules use ば, and for responses to known plans use なら.

n4-aspect-completion-preparation.heading: てしまう closes the action
n4-aspect-completion-preparation.body: てしまう marks completion, and with unintended events it carries regret or irreversibility.
examples: レポートを書いてしまいました。
財布をなくしてしまった。

n4-aspect-completion-preparation.heading: ておく prepares, てみる tries
n4-aspect-completion-preparation.body: ておく performs an action in advance for a later situation. てみる performs it as an experiment or experience.
examples: 一度食べてみてください。

n4-aspect-completion-preparation.heading: Describe one event three ways
n4-aspect-completion-preparation.body: Take a single action and express it as completed, prepared in advance, and attempted.

n4-obligation-permission.heading: Obligation uses double negatives
n4-obligation-permission.body: なければならない literally says the negative form cannot remain, which expresses obligation. Casual speech shortens it to なきゃ.
examples: 明日行かなければなりません。

n4-obligation-permission.heading: Permission and prohibition
n4-obligation-permission.body: てもいいです grants permission and てはいけない prohibits. Both build on the て-form.
examples: ここで吸ってはいけません。

n4-obligation-permission.heading: Soften prohibition in conversation
n4-obligation-permission.body: てはいけない is strong. Use ちゃだめ or explain the reason instead when speaking casually.

n3-change-and-effort.heading: ようになる describes change
n3-change-and-effort.body: ようになる states that something came to be true over time, including acquired ability with a potential verb.
examples: 日本語が話せるようになりました。

n3-change-and-effort.heading: ようにする describes effort
n3-change-and-effort.body: ようにする states deliberate effort toward a habit, and ている form presents the effort as ongoing.
examples: 毎日野菜を食べるようにしています。

n3-change-and-effort.heading: Change versus intention
n3-change-and-effort.body: Ask whether the sentence reports what happened or what someone is trying to do.

n3-decisions-and-outcomes.heading: ことにする is your decision
n3-decisions-and-outcomes.body: ことにする marks a decision made by the subject, including self-imposed rules with している.
examples: 旅行しないことにしました。

n3-decisions-and-outcomes.heading: ことになる is the outcome
n3-decisions-and-outcomes.body: ことになる presents a result produced by rules, schedules or other people, and ことになっている states a standing rule.
examples: 来月から大阪に転勤することになりました。

n3-decisions-and-outcomes.heading: Name the decision maker
n3-decisions-and-outcomes.body: Rewrite two events, choosing することに or することになる based on who decided.

n3-evidence-and-expectation.heading: らしい reports indirect evidence
n3-evidence-and-expectation.body: らしい draws a conclusion from what you saw or heard and keeps some distance from the claim.
examples: 田中さんは転職するらしい。

n3-evidence-and-expectation.heading: はず expects, かも allows doubt
n3-evidence-and-expectation.body: はず states a strong expectation from evidence, while かもしれない keeps the possibility open.
examples: もう着いているはずです。
明日は雨かもしれない。

n3-evidence-and-expectation.heading: Place the claim on a confidence scale
n3-evidence-and-expectation.body: From weakest to strongest: かもしれない, らしい, はず.

n3-formal-relations.heading: について and にとって
n3-formal-relations.body: について marks what is discussed. にとって marks the standpoint from which something is evaluated.
examples: この問題について話しましょう。
私にとって家族が一番大切です。

n3-formal-relations.heading: に対して and として
n3-formal-relations.body: に対して marks a target or a contrast. として marks the role or capacity in which someone acts.
examples: お客様に対して失礼です。
教師として働いています。

n3-formal-relations.heading: Replace English prepositions
n3-formal-relations.body: Translate four short sentences using about, for, toward and as, then justify each particle choice.

kanji-nature-elements.heading: Four pictographic kanji
kanji-nature-elements.body: 日, 月, 火 and 水 began as drawings. Recognising their shapes makes components in later kanji visible.

kanji-nature-elements.heading: From character to compound
kanji-nature-elements.body: The same kanji reappear in everyday compounds, which is why component knowledge scales.

kanji-nature-elements.heading: Inspect components
kanji-nature-elements.body: Open each kanji in the Kanji Mind Tree and note one shared component with another character.

kanji-people-and-actions.heading: Readings change by word
kanji-people-and-actions.body: 人 is じん or にん in compounds and ひと alone. Context, not the character, selects the reading.

kanji-people-and-actions.heading: Movement verbs
kanji-people-and-actions.body: 行く and 来る encode direction relative to the speaker, and both appear inside purpose patterns.

kanji-people-and-actions.heading: Connect to grammar
kanji-people-and-actions.body: The purpose pattern 〜に行く requires a motion verb, which is why these two kanji matter for grammar.

kanji-language-family.heading: The speech radical 言
kanji-language-family.body: 言 appears in a large family of characters about speaking, writing and language.

kanji-language-family.heading: 話 and 語
kanji-language-family.body: 話 adds a radical to 舌 and means talk. 語 combines 言 with 五 and 口 and appears in language names.

kanji-language-family.heading: Collect the family
kanji-language-family.body: Find two more 言 characters in the dictionary and record one word for each.

kanji-study-work.heading: Education words
kanji-study-work.body: 学 covers school and learning, and 勉強 is the standard word for study.

kanji-study-work.heading: The person who works
kanji-study-work.body: 働 pairs the person component with 動, which makes the meaning visible: a person in motion at work.

kanji-study-work.heading: Study by semantic field
kanji-study-work.body: Learning characters inside one topic creates stronger recall than memorising unrelated lists.

conversation-introductions.heading: Name and role
conversation-introductions.body: A short introduction needs です, a topic marker, and optionally an affiliation.

conversation-introductions.heading: Polite questions back
conversation-introductions.body: Ask the other person with ですか and acknowledge the answer before continuing.
examples: よろしくお願いします。

conversation-introductions.heading: Thirty-second introduction
conversation-introductions.body: Introduce yourself aloud in four sentences, then ask one question.

conversation-making-plans.heading: Invite softly
conversation-making-plans.body: ませんか is an invitation phrased as a question, so it is less pushy than a statement.

conversation-making-plans.heading: Propose and settle details
conversation-making-plans.body: ましょう proposes an action, and time and place particles complete the arrangement.
examples: 三時に駅で会いましょう。

conversation-making-plans.heading: Answering an invitation
conversation-making-plans.body: Accept with はい、行きましょう. Do not repeat the negative form back.

conversation-requests-permission.heading: Ask for help
conversation-requests-permission.body: てください is the baseline request. Add すみませんが to soften the approach.
examples: すみませんが、書いてください。

conversation-requests-permission.heading: Ask and respond
conversation-requests-permission.body: てもいいですか asks permission. Natural answers are どうぞ, いいですよ, or a soft refusal with a reason.
examples: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。
申し訳ありませんが、だめです。

conversation-requests-permission.heading: Role-play three requests
conversation-requests-permission.body: Practise one request to a friend, one to a stranger, and one permission question.

conversation-explaining-problems.heading: Describe then explain
conversation-explaining-problems.body: State what happened first, then give the reason with ので or から so the listener can follow.
examples: 電車が来ませんでした。だから、遅れました。

conversation-explaining-problems.heading: Apologise with regret
conversation-explaining-problems.body: てしまう adds the sense that something went wrong or cannot be undone, which fits an apology.
examples: 財布を忘れてしまいました。

conversation-explaining-problems.heading: Ask for advice
conversation-explaining-problems.body: Explain one problem and finish with どうしたらいいですか to request guidance.
examples: どうしたらいいですか。
